newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Clarke moves to boost private finance.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke moves to boost private finance.

text.p: Britain moved to revitalise interest in the government's flagship Private Finance Initiative (PFI) on Monday with plans allowing investors to sell their stakes, creating more liquidity in the market.

In the latest PFI revamp, Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said investors in infrastructure projects would now be able to transfer stakes to a wider range of investors, instead of being locked into terms stretching 20 to 30 years.
"We have listened. We have learned. We are taking action," he said. "PFI is a revolution in the provision of public services...after the revolution comes evolution."
Clarke was speaking at the Private Finance annual conference which included delegates from the construction and finance industries and public sector services.
PFI was set up nearly four years ago to draw private capital into public infrastructure projects ranging from roads and prisons to hospitals.

But PFI has been besieged by criticism from investing firms, builders and industry groups, including the Confederation of British Industry which claim the risks, red tape and delays are threatening to choke off fledgling interest.
Clarke said the package of measures was a response to that criticism.
On efforts to bring in new equity, he said: "It will increase the availability of capital for PFI investment. It will make PFI more liquid."

The move was welcomed in a speech due to be delivered by Neville Simms, chief executive of leading construction group Tarmac, at the conference later in the day. He said it would lead to the "recycling and reinvestment" of contractors' stakes.
The government also announced a standardised set of contract terms which will apply across all departmental projects - another item on the industry's wish list.
Clarke rejected claims the government was using PFI as a replacement for its own infrastructure spending.
"PFI is an alternative way of financing," he said, adding that the two went hand-in-hand.

But CBI director-general Adair Turner maintained: "We have concerns about cuts in public capital expenditure which have occured over the past four years, particularly in relation to public transport."

PFI has delivered 7.00 billion pounds ($11 billion) worth of projects since it started four years ago. Most have come through in the past year as only 1.5 billion pounds had been sealed this time last year. A large chunk of the total stems from the Channel Tunnel Rail Link which attracted around three billion pounds.
